paper_title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 1. Introduction Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLAs hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28 to 2.10 speedup while keeping the VLAs decoding lossless. *Equal contribution. 1 Vision-language-action models (VLAs) control robots by mapping camera images and language instruction to actions, building on pretrained vision-language models [3, 20]. Autoregressive VLAs represent continuous actions as discrete tokens and generate them by the next-token prediction used in pretraining, which lets them inherit the generalization and visuallanguage understanding of the underlying model [9, 14, 19]. The cost is speed: every action token requires forward pass of large model, limiting the control frequency. Progress in action tokenization has reduced this cost but not removed it. Early models assign one token to every action dimension at every timestep [20], whereas recent action tokenizers compress whole chunk of future actions into shorter token sequence, so that single token no longer corresponds to single action value [13, 33, 40]. The remaining tokens are still generated one at time, and this remains major bottleneck. The focus of this work is on removing this bottleneck with speculative decoding [5, 24]. lightweight draft model proposes several future tokens, and the VLA being accelerated, the target, verifies them in one parallel pass and accepts the longest prefix that matches its own predictions. Because only matching tokens are accepted, decoding is lossless through exact verification by the target. This property is valuable in robot control: the accelerated policy uses lossless decoding, with no tolerance to tune and exact verification of action tokens. The speedup, however, depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted per verification cycle, which is low for robot actions. Many different tokens encode nearly the same motion, so draft close to the correct action is still rejected when its tokens differ. Existing speculative decoding methods for VLAs relax verification by accepting drafted tokens that are sufficiently close to the targets predictions [44, 48, 49]. These acceptance rules rely on per-dimension action bins, where neighboring bins correspond to nearby values of the same action dimension [3, 20]. This notion of proximity does not directly extend to compressed tokenizers such as FAST [40] and ActionCodec [13], which require the complete token sequence before decoding it into an action chunk. Direct comparison with the targets decoded actions would require the target to generate the remaining tokens of the action chunk before acceptance can be decided. In other words, relaxing acceptance for single token would require the target to generate the entire remaining action sequence. Token embedding distance offers an alternative that can be evaluated immediately, but we find that it is an unreliable proxy for action distance. Ranking candidate tokens by embedding distance disagrees with ranking them by decoded action distance for about 31% of pairs, and 18% of single-token substitutions in complete FAST sequences do not decode to valid action at all  (Fig. 4)  . When verification is relaxed by embedding distance on π0-FAST, raising the speedup from 1.60 to 1.90 lowers the success rate from 91.7% to 71.4% (Tab. 4). This raises our question: can speculative decoding be effective for VLAs with compressed action tokenizers while keeping verification exact? To this end, we introduce VSpark, which keeps verification exact and instead exploits the similarity between actions on the draft side  (Fig. 1)  . If many tokens encode nearly the same motion, then the draft should learn from more than token labels, and rejected token is often nearly right, so what the target predicted after it remains informative. VSpark builds on the parallel drafter DSpark [10] and rests on three design choices. First, we train the draft on rollouts collected with calibrated action noise. Drafts are usually trained only on the states visited by the training demonstrations. We adapt noise injection in DART [22] to draft training by perturbing actions during target rollouts in simulation. DART calibrates noise to discrepancies between learned policys actions and those of supervisor, such as human expert. We instead use discrepancies between draft and target actions, setting the noise scale to reflect the drafts errors in predicting the target. Second, we introduce feature alignment. Supervision by token labels treats every wrong token alike, however close its action is to the correct one. We therefore feed the targets hidden features to the draft and train it to regress them, giving it continuous signal that token identity alone does not provide. This raises the average number of tokens committed per verification cycle from 3.22 to 3.87 on π0-FAST (Tab. 7). Third, we propose continuation reuse. When the target verifies tree of candidates, it also computes what it would predict after each rejected candidate, and standard decoding discards these predictions. We consider draft tokens that match the targets predictions after rejected token: In VLAs, 45% to 55% of these tokens also match the targets predictions under the corrected prefix (Tab. 5). Continuation reuse promotes these predictions into the next draft tree, where they are verified again, ensuring lossless decoding at no extra cost to the target. Acting purely at inference time, continuation reuse requires no training and no change to either model. The outcome of these design choices is that VSpark accelerates four autoregressive VLAs, π0-FAST, StarVLA-FAST, ActionCodec, and G0.5, which together cover frequency-based and learned vector-quantized action tokenizers. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and SimplerEnv, it achieves 1.28 to 2.10 speedup over autoregressive decoding while retaining exact verification of action tokens. Under the same exact verification, VSpark outperforms five recent speculative decoding methods [7, 10, 17, 18, 28] on every model and benchmark. This shows that similarity between robot actions can be turned into speed while retaining exact verification. 2. Related Works Action tokenization converts continuous robot actions into discrete tokens that an autoregressive VLA can predict, and maps the generated tokens back into actions. Tokenizers fall into two categories. Per-dimension tokenizers discretize each action dimension into bins: OpenVLA [20] predicts seven tokens per control step, three for translation, three for rotation, and one for the gripper. Compressed tokenizers instead encode chunk of actions jointly across dimensions and timesteps, which shortens the sequence. FAST [40] applies discrete cosine transform to the chunk, quantizes the coefficients, and compresses them with byte-pair encoding. ActionCodec [13] and G0.5 [33] learn discrete representation with neural encoder and vector quantization, using residual quantization to refine the reconstruction. With compressed tokenizer, token carries information from several dimensions and timesteps, and the action is recovered only after the whole sequence is decoded. We evaluate VSpark on VLAs with both kinds of compressed tokenizers. Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation with lossless decoding by verifying multiple draft tokens in one target pass [5, 24]. Tree verification checks several alternative continuations in the same pass [4, 37]. Developed for large language models, this line of work has concentrated on the draft model, which falls into two categories. Autoregressive drafters run once for every drafted token: EAGLE [26] drafts with single Transformer block that predicts the targets hidden features, EAGLE-2 [27] builds the draft tree dynamically from cumulative draft scores, and EAGLE-3 [28] removes feature regression and trains on draft-generated contexts with multi-layer target features. Parallel drafters instead predict all positions in 2 one pass: P-EAGLE [17] and PARD [1, 2] replace the unavailable preceding tokens with learned or mask embeddings, and DFlash [7] uses bidirectional attention within masked block, injecting target features as keys and values in every draft layer. Because such predictions do not depend on the tokens chosen at earlier positions, DSpark [10], DFlash2 [18], and Domino [16] add lightweight sequential corrections conditioned on the preceding tokens. Recent work also constructs draft trees from parallel drafters by selecting high-probability branches from the per-position distributions [30, 31, 41, 47, 50]. Other work reuses target predictions or hidden states that would otherwise be discarded after verification to improve subsequent drafts in large language models [21, 36]. Speculative decoding has also been extended to vision-language models that generate text [23, 29, 38]. VSpark builds on DSpark and differs in three respects: it injects calibrated action noise during rollouts, restores the feature supervision that EAGLE-3 removed, and fills the draft tree with target-predicted continuations rather than draft predictions alone. Speculative decoding for action policies applies this procedure to the action tokens generated by VLA. Existing methods use the tree decoding of EAGLE-2 and relax the verification rule, accepting drafted token that differs from the targets prediction when the two are sufficiently close. Spec-VLA [44] accepts drafted token when its action bin lies within fixed distance of the targets. KERV [48] adjusts this tolerance with kinematic information and uses Kalman filter to predict the remaining action dimensions after rejection. HeiSD [49] switches between drafts retrieved from the training data and drafts generated by draft model according to the recent robot motion, and accelerates retrieved drafts by skipping verification and relaxing acceptance over groups of action tokens. WA-SpecDec [45] injects world-model features into fine-tuned target to make relaxed acceptance more reliable, and observes that the deviations it admits are most harmful near contact. Verification has also been used to decide how much of an action chunk to execute [6], and speculative inference has been explored for diffusion-based VLAs [34, 39], which generate continuous actions and fall outside token-level verification. The token-level methods above are all developed on the per-dimension binning of OpenVLA and relax or skip verification. Comparing decoded actions with compressed tokenizers requires autoregressively generating the complete target action chunk, negating speculative gains. VSpark instead maintains strict verification for lossless acceleration. 3. Method Given an observation and language instruction, VSpark uses lossless decoding for the target VLAs action tokens, using fewer forward passes of the target. As shown in Fig. 2, it changes how the draft is trained (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3) and which candidates are verified in each cycle (Sec. 3.4), leaving the target, the action tokenizer, and the verification rule untouched. 3.1. We call this model the target Mt, and the lightweight model that drafts tokens for it the draft Md. Speculative decoding with draft trees. Speculative decoding replaces the sequential passes of the target by smaller number of verification cycles. In each cycle, the draft proposes tree of candidate tokens that extends the tokens confirmed so far, the confirmed prefix. Each node holds one candidate token, and the path from the root to node is the context in which that token is proposed. Candidates are expanded according to the draft probabilities, and the nodes with the highest cumulative log probabilities are kept within fixed node budget. The target then verifies all nodes in single forward pass, using tree attention mask that restricts each node to the confirmed prefix, its ancestors, and itself. Under greedy decoding, verification walks down the tree from the root, following at each step the child that equals the targets prediction. When no child matches, the targets prediction is appended as correction token; when all proposals on the path match, one additional token predicted by the target is appended. The accepted tokens extend the confirmed prefix, which is the context for the next cycle. In standard tree decoding, all branches outside the accepted path are discarded, together with the predictions that the target computed for them. DSpark. We build on DSpark [10], parallel drafter. Rollouts start from simulator states in the training data. At each observation, the frozen target generates action tokens and hidden features. We decode the tokens, add the calibrated noise to the translation and rotation commands, clip them to the valid action range, and leave the gripper command unchanged. Continuation Reuse The purpose of continuation reuse is to exploit predictions that the target has already computed and that standard decoding discards. When drafted token is rejected, the target has still predicted what would follow it. If the rejected token and the token the target wanted encode similar motions, what follows is likely to be the same, and it can be proposed in the next cycle  (Fig. 3)  . Constructing draft trees. Exactness. Continuation reuse changes only which candidates are proposed. Following common practice for autoregressive VLAs, we use greedy decoding: the target verifies every candidate under its actual prefix and accepts only tokens matching its highest-probability prediction. Promoted continuations are verified again under the corrected prefix, and only the accepted path enters the confirmed prefix, ensuring lossless decoding. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Target VLAs. We accelerate four publicly released autoregressive VLAs that cover two families of action tokenizer. π0-FAST and StarVLA-FAST [12] use FAST tokenization, and ActionCodec-AR and G0.5 use learned vector-quantized tokenizers. The main results cover all four, while the ablations and analyses use one model per family, π0-FAST and ActionCodec. Speculative decoding baselines. We compare VSpark with five speculative decoding methods: EAGLE-3 [28], P-EAGLE [17], DFlash [7], DFlash2 [18], and DSpark [10]. Every method accelerates the same frozen targets, so the methods differ only in their draft. We adapt each to action tokens and extend the parallel drafters to trees, so that all are verified alike. Benchmarks. LIBERO comprises four suites, Goal, Spatial, Object, and Long, each with ten tasks and 50 initial states per task, giving 500 episodes per model and suite. LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro evaluate the same suites under distribution shift: LIBERO-Plus perturbs camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, lighting, backgrounds, sensor noise, and object layouts, and LIBERO-Pro varies objects, positions, language semantics, tasks, and environments. SimplerEnv (WidowX) evaluates different embodiment, using StarVLAFAST trained on BridgeData V2 on four tasks with 24 episodes each. We follow the official protocol of each benchmark. Metrics. We report the acceptance length τ, the average number of tokens committed per verification cycle including the correction or additional token, and the speedup, the autoregressive decoding time of the target divided by the speculative decoding time in the same setting. Tab. 1 compares VSpark with the baselines on the four LIBERO suites. VSpark achieves the highest acceptance length and speedup on every model and suite, with average speedups of 1.93, 1.61, 2.10, and 1.28 on π0-FAST, StarVLA-FAST, ActionCodec, and G0.5. Conclusion Effect of verification strategy and draft depth. Tab. 6 compares verifying single chain with verifying tree, and one-layer with five-layer drafts. Trees help every method, as exact matching of action tokens is hard and tree offers the target several candidates at each position. VSpark benefits the most, since continuation reuse operates only on trees: its τ rises from 2.28 to 3.94 on π0-FAST and from 2.46 to 4.21 on ActionCodec, and its speedup from 1.31 to 1.93 and from 1.44 to 2.10. Deeper drafts, common in DFlash-based methods, do not pay off. With five layers, the acceptance length of VSpark changes little (3.94 to 3.92 and 4.21 to 4.33), while We presented VSpark, speculative decoding framework that provides lossless acceleration for autoregressive VLAs. Its premise is that the similarity between robot actions should be exploited when drafting rather than when verifying: calibrated-noise rollouts and feature alignment teach the draft more than token labels can, and continuation reuse recycles predictions that the target has already made along rejected branches, at no additional cost. With exact verification, VSpark is the fastest of six speculative decoders on every model and benchmark we tested, including targets on which most baselines are slower than autoregressive decoding. Despite these gains, 8 VSpark has limitations that follow from its design. Hybrid attention has cost: recurrent states in the linear attention layers of G0.5 complicate parallel tree verification, potentially limiting speedup despite improved acceptance. Continuation reuse helps only when rejection leaves the continuation unchanged, which holds for about half of the rejections and varies with the tokenizer. Finally, VSpark helps target trained on real-robot data (WidowX), but collecting noisy rollouts on real robot without simulator requires further study. Improving parallel verification for hybrid attention architectures and collecting noise rollouts without simulator remain directions for future work.

We compare SpecVLA [44], KERV [48], DSpark, and VSpark on LIBERO Goal over 500 episodes per setting.3 We use the public SpecVLA4 and KERV5 implementations. Both SpecVLA and KERV use the EAGLE-2 [27] draft architecture. For SpecVLA, we use its publicly released draft checkpoint. KERV follows the same draft training approach as SpecVLA, with matching draft architecture and optimizer settings in their public implementations. Since KERV draft checkpoint is not explicitly provided, we use the public SpecVLA checkpoint with KERVs implementation. Evaluation protocol. OpenVLA generates seven tokens per action. The public SpecVLA implementation checks the stopping condition only after committing full accepted block, allowing tokens beyond this boundary to be counted and inflating the reported acceptance length. We correct this behavior by limiting generation and acceptance-length accounting to the seven action tokens. Before the correction, our reproduction yielded acceptance lengths of 2.03 under strict verification and 2.95 under relaxed verification, close to the results reported by SpecVLA. After the correction, these decrease to 1.70 and 2.38, respectively, as reported in Tab. B.12. Strict denotes exact verification.
